questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals of Algebraic Functions Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
Let $u={x}^{2}-1.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,x\,\text{d}x=\frac{\text{d}u}{2}.
$$

We also note that
${x}^{2}=u+1.$

Now we can solve the integral in terms of $u,$ and then express our final answer in terms of $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3}\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{2}\cdot \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (u+1)\cdot \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int (u+1){u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int ({u}^{3/2}+{u}^{1/2})\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}+\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2})+C \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\sqrt{({x}^{2}-1)^{5}}+\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{({x}^{2}-1)^{3}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $u=3x+1.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that
$x=\frac{u-1}{3}.$

Now we can solve the integral in terms of $u,$ and then express our final answer in terms of $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\sqrt{3x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{u-1}{3}\cdot \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int ({u}^{3/2}-{u}^{1/2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(\frac{1}{5/2}{u}^{5/2}-\frac{1}{3/2}{u}^{3/2})+C \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(\frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}-\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2})+C \\  & =\frac{2}{45}{u}^{5/2}-\frac{2}{27}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{45}\sqrt{(3x+1)^{5}}-\frac{2}{27}\sqrt{(3x+1)^{3}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $u=x+1,$ which integral is equivalent to $\int \frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $u=x+1,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

We also note that 
$x=u-1.$

Now we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{(u-1)^{2}}{\sqrt{u}}\text{d}u \\  & =\int ({u}^{2}-2u+1){u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int ({u}^{3/2}-2{u}^{1/2}+{u}^{-1/2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int (\sqrt{{u}^{3}}-2\sqrt{u}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}})\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $u=4-x.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that
$x=4-u.$

Now we can solve the integral in terms of $u,$ and then express our final answer in terms of $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2x+1)\sqrt{4-x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2(4-u)+1)\sqrt{u}(-\text{d}u) \\  & =-\int (9-2u)\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\int (9{u}^{1/2}-2{u}^{3/2})\text{d}u \\  & =-(6{u}^{3/2}-\frac{4}{5}{u}^{5/2})+C \\  & =-6\sqrt{(4-x)^{3}}+\frac{4}{5}\sqrt{(4-x)^{5}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

$x=u+2.$

Now we can solve the integral in terms of $u,$ and then express our final answer in terms of $x:$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Definite Integrals of Algebraic Functions Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
Let $u=6x+6.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that $x=\frac{1}{6}(u-6).$ 

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $-1$ | $1/3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $0$ | $8$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1/3}\frac{7}{4}x\sqrt[3]{6x+6}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{8}\frac{7}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{6}(u-6)\cdot {u}^{1/3}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{7}{144}{\int }_{0}^{8}({u}^{4/3}-6{u}^{1/3})\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{7}{144}{(\frac{1}{(7/3)}{u}^{7/3}-6\cdot \frac{1}{(4/3)}{u}^{4/3})|}_{0}^{8} \\  & =\frac{7}{144}{(\frac{3}{7}{u}^{7/3}-\frac{9}{2}{u}^{4/3})|}_{0}^{8} \\  & =\frac{7}{144}[(\frac{3}{7}\cdot {8}^{7/3}-\frac{9}{2}\cdot {8}^{4/3})-(\frac{3}{7}\cdot {0}^{7/3}-\frac{9}{2}\cdot {0}^{4/3})] \\  & =\frac{7}{144}(\frac{384}{7}-72) \\  & =\frac{7}{144}\cdot (-\frac{120}{7}) \\  & =-\frac{5}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $u=2x-1$, which integral is equivalent to ${\int }_{1}^{3}x\sqrt{2x-1}\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $u=2x-1$, then we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that $x=\frac{u+1}{2}.$ 

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $1$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $1$ | $5$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}x\sqrt{2x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{u+1}{2}\cdot \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{5}(u+1){u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{5}({u}^{3/2}+{u}^{1/2})\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Definite Integrals of Algebraic Functions Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
Let $u=x+2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that $x=u-2.$

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $-2$ | $0$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $0$ | $2$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{0}x{(x+2)}^{3}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(u-2){u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({u}^{4}-2{u}^{3})\,\text{d}u \\  & ={(\frac{1}{5}{u}^{5}-2\cdot \frac{1}{4}{u}^{4})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{5}{u}^{5}-\frac{1}{2}{u}^{4})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}({2}^{5}-{0}^{5})-\frac{1}{2}({2}^{4}-{0}^{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(32-0)-\frac{1}{2}(16-0) \\  & =\frac{32}{5}-8 \\  & =-\frac{8}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals of Algebraic Functions Using Substitution
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $u = x^2+1.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral in terms of $u,$ and then express our final answer in terms of $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{2}\cdot x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}\,\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \overset{u-1}{\overset{⏞}{{x}^{2}}}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot \overset{\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u}{\overset{⏞}{x\,\text{d}x}} \\  & =\int (u-1)\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int (u-1){u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int ({u}^{3/2}-{u}^{1/2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}-\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2})+C \\  & =\frac{1}{5}({x}^{2}+1)^{5/2}-\frac{1}{3}({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{5}}-\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Definite Integrals of Algebraic Functions Using Substitution
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $u=1-2x.$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad -\dfrac 1 2 \,\textrm d u = \textrm d x.
$$

We also note that $x = \dfrac 1 2 (1-u).$ 

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $0$ | $1/2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $1$ | $0$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}x(1-2x)^{5}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{0}\frac{1}{2}\cdot (1-u)\cdot {u}^{5}\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{0}(1-u)\cdot {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{0}({u}^{5}-{u}^{6})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}{(\frac{1}{6}{u}^{6}-\frac{1}{7}{u}^{7})|}_{1}^{0} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}([0-0]-[\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{7}]) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}(-\frac{1}{42}) \\  & =\frac{1}{168}\end{aligned}
$$
